utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I understand there is some matters you want to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just short administrative matters, and probably better raised first thing in the morning rather than at the end of the afternoon. I suspect we are not going to have a full day's evidence in any event, and therefore better if we organise these things now. It will only take a few minutes, one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if we are in private session already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We want to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it probably safer to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we do, tomorrow, unless there is any objection, we shall sit at 9 and finish at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So there is one more witness about a checkpoint. He's been -- his statement has been served on the Defence some time ago, and I've notified them that he is, of course, a witness we intend to call. Last point, rather more substantial in a sense: There are a number of witnesses who, in our last amended overview of witnesses, we indicated were witnesses whose transcripts could and should be adduced, and who needn't give evidence directly. For example, there is a man called Remi Landry, whose transcript is identified. We've had no response, and there are a number of witnesses here as to our proposal made clear on that amended overview. We've had no response as to whether those transcripts can be read, and it's becoming pressing that we do have a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be helpful if you would, today, identify those who you wish to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that the Defence can know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber will remember the tabulated document, the amended overview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And they are all there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's dated the 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right. And they are all identified there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am not sure, looking at it, I can follow which one it is. It may be simplest if you just identify those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, it's not to be called transcript; I think NTBT, but never mind. The next witness is a witness who has given evidence before, on two different occasions, and under two different settings. I am happy to say that, and probably much to his credit, he doesn't seek protection. And I'll call him now to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court. May I have one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Relative to the transcript witnesses, please just give us a list and we'll respond. I can't read it from the overview. Relative to the new witness they want to add, that will be in the same situation as Mr. Beese. We were given his statement on December 9. Maybe we can argue both of those tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or even this afternoon, if we run out of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because the producer of the maps is not in a position, I think, to give the evidence today or tomorrow, and the witness who can assist us with the overview is not available today, but will be available tomorrow, if that's the position reach.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The other two matters are there is apparently a video, fly-by video of the valley that they want introduced. We have not seen it. We need to see it and go over it with Mr. Kordic. To do that requires some co-operation with the detention centre and some advance planning. The sooner we can get it, the better. He's clearly in a better position to determine what it is than we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is that video available?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's certainly a copy of it available, and I'll make it available to them as soon as I can. Mid-morning break, I should think, is a probability. I'll check with Ms. Bauer, who is dealing with it this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When we get it, I understand we'll need some intervention from the Court relative to the detention centre, but I'll work the details of that with the legal officer. Last but not least, would Your Honour please consider that we now have about three and a half linear feet of documents to review from the Prosecution, with more coming. Would you also please consider that as a result of the ex parte applications, we're starting to get that which we sought for some time from third parties and other people involved in producing documents and things relative to the former Yugoslavia, and of course we're busily working on a motion to dismiss for the close of the case, my point being, to throw another egg on the pile, the more time Your Honour can give us in the schedule between the close of the Prosecution's case and the beginning of our case would be greatly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, just for the record, the first matter my colleague raised, the issue of the tape, we do not have a position on that issue, since it is irrelevant for my client. As to the second issue raised related to the tapes which will show us the Lasva Valley, I of course join what my colleague said, because it will be very difficult for us to make any comment on that material unless the client will see it himself. That is a critical point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt you can make arrangements, too, with the Prosecution to have a copy, if there is one, or share one with Mr. Kordic's counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. With regard to this witness, I do not mind him being led through a number of questions, except 8, 14, 16 and 17. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness come in? Just harking back to the question of transcript witnesses, I thought I had prepared myself a little better for this than I was allowed to recall. The very last two pages of the amended overview of witnesses, pages 21 and 22, have those transcript witnesses extracted and separately listed, so I'll make that available, in a copy form, if they haven't got the document with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Give us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Ibrahim Nuhagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, before the conflict, were you resident in Ocehnici, which was a purely Muslim town in the Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think there was some nine Muslim families there in a total of some eight houses.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Quite true, eight households. How many members, I wouldn't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness have on the ELMO I think the only exhibit in his evidence, which is Z1694. It is an extract from a map with which we are familiar, and if we look at the bottom of the map off the screen at the moment -- if the usher could help us; thank you very much -- Mr. Nuhagic, do we see "Ocehnici" written across an area close to Donja Polje?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was Ocehnici close to the Draga barracks?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Under whose control were they before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: The HVO's.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 27th of January of 1993, did HVO soldiers come to your village, they searched the village, and did they confiscate all weapons, including hunting rifles as well as machine guns?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms, HVO flashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they have anything on their faces?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: The majority of them had masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were all the men in the village detained and taken, via the police station at Busovaca, to Kaonik camp, which we can see at the top of the map?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: During that time, that is, the time of passage from Ocehnici to Kaonik, did you have to keep your arms behind your heads?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: We did, all the way to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you mistreated in some way and were you the subject of threats?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the mistreatment and what were the threats?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: The mistreatment meant beating. The threats, that they would cut off our ears or slit our throats. But mostly blows all the way to the bus, and we could not get on to the bus without being hit, without being struck by them. And then again as we were getting off the bus, they would beat us once again, because there were two lines of soldiers, soldiers lined up in two lines, and as we got off, they would beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think there was a batch of soldiers who came from a vehicle, which had a mounted gun on it, which were particularly bad at the beating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the bus stop in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, when these things were happening in Busovaca, were there pedestrians on the street able to see what was going on or not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: It was night-time. There were only HVO troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In Kaonik, is it the case that you were not beaten, but that you heard other prisoners screaming?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I was beaten on the way and my back was hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you learn of other prisoners being taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Most of them went to dig trenches, or most all of their able-bodied, except for myself, because I had been hit, and a few people under age who did not go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the International Committee of the Red Cross intervene, and were the prisoners, including yourself, released at the beginning of February?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did come, but they were not released immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But eventually?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In April, namely, on the 16th of April, could you both hear and see shooting taking place near to where you lived?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, one could see from Kula, Polom, Solakovici, and other places, that is where there was fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know or know of a man called Mirko Cosic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was his function at the time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: He had a unit, an intervention unit called Jokers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see that man in April of 1993, on the television?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the bus stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was he saying on the broadcast you saw?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Those announcers, or cameramen, asked him whether the troops, whether those fighters obeyed him. And he said they obeyed him very well indeed and were doing their job. And he mentioned Polom, Kula, Loncari, as those who had done their job particularly well. And the cameraman asked him, what was that job, what did they do, and he said with time will show.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 19th of April of 1993, were you in your village when soldiers came again?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How were they dressed? What units did they come from?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: All I know is this Nikica Grubesic was their chief commander. But what were they, what were those units? They were HVO fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms. Military with HVO patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you say anything about masks or not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Masks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did they attack on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, they simply came, entered the village and, whenever they found somebody, they killed. They immediately set houses on fire, killed the livestock in stables. Those who managed to escape, they did, but they slew all others they found. And my neighbours, those who survived, they were in a shelter, and so that they couldn't find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When they set alight the houses, how did they do that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: They mostly used incinerating ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were you precisely at the time of this attack?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I was -- it just happened that I was in an outside Nuhagici. And as I was coming out, my niece, standing outside the front door of my house, told me, "Uncle, get away, so that you do not come with us." And that is what I did. I began to flee and they opened fire after me. I don't know how many bullets they fired. But I began to run in eights, that is, to run in zigzag, so that I fell. And that Croat fighter who was firing at me thought that I -- that he had hit me and that I had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think, in due course, you returned to your own house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I went back to my own house at night, when everything was quiet, when nothing could be heard, and it was dark. That's when I went back to my own house, to see the -- my family members who had been killed: my mother, my sister, my brothers, two daughters, who had stayed on in my house. But when I got to the house, you could only see the embers. They had tried to flee from the house, but there was a burst of gunfire and they were hit from the house. So that they burnt to death. I have seen -- I saw a great deal of trouble and had a very hard time putting out what remained of the fire. My uncle turned up and he told me to take care of myself, because what had happened, had happened, and could not be put right. But I thought, when I saw these victims of mine, I wished that I had been among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you listed the family members. Your wife was --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. My mother, my wife, my sister, and my brother's two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The uncle who spoke to you, did he tell you that he had been trying to get the livestock out of his burning barn and had been shot?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, from my yard. They shot at him when he turned up in his own yard to go to his shed to save the cattle. And they shot at him and wounded him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he tell you that his relations had been killed by a burst of fire when they tried to run away from their house?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it you who heard the HVO soldiers looking for him, asking where he had hidden, or did he tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard, because I was down by my house and his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of this attack, did you hear soldiers speaking to each other, and if so, what names did you hear them using?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, most of them were nicknames, like Zara, Kole. So there were nicknames: Cigo and others. They were all nicknames, and I know them by heart, all these nicknames, and the real surnames.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know any of them as individuals? Did you actually know who they were?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew them from before, but as they had masks on, as they were wearing masks --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the man Zarko, was he also known as Cigo or Cigo?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man Zeljo, who was he?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Zeljo Vujica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a man, Zarko Cosic, or was that the same name?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Kologranic, not Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there was Mladjo?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Kologranic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he known by another name as well?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No. Mostly he was known as Kole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a Zarko Kologranic, or not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, those are the three brothers, yes: Kole, Ranko and Zeljo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before this attack, had you heard of something that that man Zarko Cosic had said?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, several days before that, he was in the village. And he said, if anything happens to any member of his family, if he were to be wounded or anything, our village would be burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To whom did he say that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: He told my sister that, my sister that was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think following that attack, you spent some three months in the house of a relation in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: In Busovaca and Skradno, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were, I think, expelled from where you were living on at least three times, or three times, by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to tell us, please, how you learned of who had done this attack. Don't tell us immediately who it was, who, as you understood it, was in charge of the attack. Tell us, first of all, how you heard about it. From whom did you learn who was responsible for the attack?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: For the attack, well, it could have been none other than Dusko Grubesic, who was in command with a unit. And Dusko, we know who Dusko receives his assignments from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, before we come to those names, really, I wanted you to tell the Judges how you learned about it or how you knew that to be the case. Just explain how you would know that. Is it something that somebody told you or was it something that you saw yourself? Just explain it so that they can follow.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know -- I didn't actually understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My fault. The Judges will want to know how it is that you knew who was in charge of this attack. Can you help us? Is it something that somebody else told you or was it something you could work out yourself from what you saw of the soldiers? Just explain it, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the only thing that I saw was on television. I saw Zoran Maric when he said that in the area, only one plant should be allowed to grow. And we couldn't understand that until the events that took place happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you -- this is paragraph 18, Your Honours -- when did you see Zoran Maric, who I think was the president of the Busovaca municipality, when did you see him saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it was when the soldiers took their oath at the Busovaca stadium. That was when he read that out, what should be done, what they should do. And that's the only thing that I remember, because I didn't watch television, nor did I have time to watch it, because I was outside mostly farming, and of course much more of that could have been seen had I had the time to watch television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you tell us that Dusko Grubesic was responsible. Why do you say that? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, he was the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And how do you know that it was that unit? Name the unit, please, and then: How do you know that it was that unit that committed these killings?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How near was this unit to Ocehnici at the time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the command in Busovaca was, say, two and a half to three kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you understand why Dusko Grubesic ordered the attack, what the reason was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know of any other names of people who were involved in this attack as leaders, commanders, or whatever else?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, only Pasko Ljubicic. That was the leader of the group in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I learned that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From whom did you learn it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, from my own -- well, my people and some of the soldiers that I was acquainted with. We would meet on the street and we would sort of chat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say "some of their soldiers," is this soldiers who told you they had been involved in the attack or was this soldiers who told you they had learned themselves about the attack?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No, they did not take part. The ones that did not take part in the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And in which group or unit were the soldiers who told you these things?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, they were in that same unit of that Nikica Grubesic person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that the Zrinjski Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was anything said about a connection between something that had happened at the Draga barracks and this attack?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My fault again. When you heard about what had happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting, but we have a comment to make with respect to this. We are dealing with multiple hearsay. The witness answered this question. He said he did not know the reasons why the commander issued orders for an attack on the village. He said that quite certainly, and now I have the feeling that they wish to bring him back to the same question. So that is my objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're dealing with a witness who has understandable difficulties in following the technicalities of question-answering in court, and I hope the question that I asked is not in any sense offensively leading or tendentious and gives him an opportunity to refresh his memory of something that I have reason to believe he will be able to tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think the fairest question is to repeat the earlier question: "Do you know any reason that there may have been for this attack?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You heard the learned Judge's question, Mr. Nuhagic. Do you know of any reason that there may have been for this attack?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: The reason is that -- and we should be quite clear about that. It was not only my village, but this happened elsewhere as well, that it should have been cleansed of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I'm going to move on, then, Your Honour. Paragraph 14 in the summary --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise once again for interrupting, but with respect to this particular paragraph, we also say that this is multiple hearsay. We consider that in this case, too, the provisions of Article 80(D) should be applied, because I think that in order to ensure a fair trial, that is far more important than the probative value of this particular paragraph. 89(D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's hear the foundation for the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the paragraph, as drafted, may be a little misleading, and it may be the material is rather more direct than appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, do you know a woman called Hasija Beslic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just "yes" or "no" to this question. Was there an occasion that you can recall when you were talking about her -- with her about what are called safety papers or papers that had been issued for Muslims? And again, just answer the question "yes" or "no." Was there an occasion when you had a discussion with her about those papers?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had that document too, and regardless, everybody had those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you and she see and talk to someone else about those papers on the occasion that you discussed matters with her?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So now approaching it in a little more detail, the papers were issued by who and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what were the papers supposed to do? What were they supposed to achieve?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, when the soldiers would come in the evening or during the day, we were supposed to show those papers so that they should not disturb us; that is to say, the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your experience, were the papers effective in what they set out to do?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The conversation you had with Hasija Beslic, what was the topic of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, we talked, and I was present when -- with Dario Kordic, because they knew one another in the same company. They worked in the Vatrostalna company together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... and Dario Kordic knew one another?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what did she say to him about the papers, and what, if anything, did he reply?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, she said that the papers, the documents were worthless, that they weren't -- that they were useless. It was -- they weren't serving their purpose. And he said that they would be worth something because what had happened would not happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did she give him any examples of what had happened, in contravention to the protection that the papers should have given?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. She told him that they were worthless, because soldiers still came up and expelled people from houses, and would send several families out of a house. And he said that this would not happen in the future, but the next night, and the night after that, and after that, things were repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At whose house; your house or at houses of other people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, my relations' houses. And I was expelled from the three houses: from the first, the second and the third, all my relatives' houses. And from the third house, we were all expelled and went to Skradno. We were taken there, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you were expelled, was anything said about the report or complaint that you'd made to Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers said -- told us, when they came to expel us from our houses, they said, "You complain to Kordic, to Dario Kordic. He gave you security papers, whereas in fact he allowed us to do what we are doing now."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those soldiers, do you know anything about the unit from which they came?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the unit of Dusko Grubesic, Zrinjski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This whole incident, the incident with Hasija Beslic and the couple of nights that followed, roughly when was that? Can you help us? What month, if you can. If you can't, don't guess.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in June, perhaps the beginning of July, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In August 1993, were you taken from where you were then living to the village of Skradno?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: They took me and my relatives, yes, three of my relatives, and with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While in Skradno, was the area patrolled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And while there, were men taken to dig trenches in Kula, Strane and Bare, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am aware of that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You yourself, were you taken trench digging, or were you allowed to stay in Skradno?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I was injured, and, as I was getting old in age, they didn't take me, but they took the younger ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Throughout this period of time, did you watch television from time to time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We weren't able to because we didn't have any electricity; we didn't have all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, probably my fault for the way I asked the question. The whole period of time, starting from before the first detention, did you see Busovaca television at all?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in 1993, and in 1992. It was expressly Busovaca television, from 4.00 to 6.00 in the afternoon. And there was nothing else to watch. It was HTV, Croatian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see Kordic on the television, ever?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who were the other leading political or military figures that you recall seeing on the television?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Dario Kordic, Blaskic, Tihomir Blaskic, Ignac Kostroman, Anto Valenta.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What position or rank did Kordic have, so far as you could judge, in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like this, you see. He would go step by step upwards. I didn't hear his rank, but I heard tell that he came up to the rank of colonel, rose to the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say it was a step-by-step progress. Where do you recall his starting? And in what organisation?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, he started from a municipal clerk, an ordinary municipal clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you at any stage aware of his involvement in any political party, and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I know before, in the company he worked in, he was a member of the Communist Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And on the television, on Busovaca television, was he associated with any political party or grouping?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No. Later on, in 1993, and in 1992, the middle of 1992, when there was all the bombing by the former army, the Serbian army, then he started wearing a uniform and became a military man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of the television programmes, that's the Busovaca television programmes, was there anything said generally about the state of Croatia itself that you can recall, or not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. The only thing that I do remember is that when we were sent off to the camps, some of the soldiers would shout out that this was Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you recall a particular news broadcast where something was said about potatoes?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When was this, and who was speaking?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: It was in the month of June, the beginning of June, when Dario said that we should plant as many potatoes as possible. But when the time for harvest comes, then it would be decided who would reap the benefits of the harvest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the potatoes that were being planted had been provided by whom; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: From humanitarian aid, some of them would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you wait there, you may be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was waiting for your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, may I introduce myself. I am Mitko Naumovski, an attorney from Zagreb, one of the Defence counsel for Mr. Kordic, and I have a number of questions for you. In view of the fact that we understand one another when we speak, wait a few minutes before giving your answer, for my question to be interpreted into English and French. And I will do the same. Mr. Nuhagic, a few brief questions regarding the actual position of your village. You lived in the village of Ocenici, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And did your part of the village have a special name, that is Nuhagici?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In this part of the village there were about eight houses in all, Muslim households?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And in another part of the village, another part of the same village of Ocenici, who lived there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: The Vujica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So they were Croatian families?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: How many houses did they have?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Four houses. Those that were closest to my part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: To the west of your village was a large forest area called Polom, was there not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the HVO defence lines went along the western edges towards the woods in Polom in January '93?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In view of the geographic position of the village, there wasn't a traditional front line, but there were just patrols?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No. It was a classic front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that there were troops there, stationed permanently?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in January '93, how many young men from Nuhagici had left the village, before the events that you described?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And those five men, can we agree that they were members of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: While we were in the village, they kept guard duty, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And in January they left the village to go to Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, to Fojnica, Kacuni, depending where people had relatives, family members, relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in January, therefore, before the events of the 27th, on the other side of the front line held by the HVO, were soldiers belonging to the Territorial Defence, who held positions facing the HVO positions?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, because I was in an area controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I know that you were not a military person, as you have already told us, but perhaps you can answer a question regardless of your lack of military expertise. In the course of the night, would these young men come to your village in secret?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please, very briefly, a couple of questions regarding your detention in the Kaonik prison. Since you were injured, you were taken to see a doctor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You were taken to the medical centre in Busovaca, were you not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: During your detention in Kaonik, nobody hurt you, and they treated you relatively well, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I think that you have already told us that you were not taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I did not, because I was injured. I went to see a doctor, and then I was taken back to the barracks. But I didn't dare say what had happened to me. I lied. I said that I had fallen in the barn when I was feeding the cattle. If I had said the truth, then I would have suffered in the same way as the other detainees. I would have been beaten again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, nobody told you that you should lie; that was your own decision?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I could not -- I couldn't even go to see the doctor on my own to tell the doctor the truth. I was not alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Let us go on to another topic, and that is the attack in April, as you described it. You mentioned a person called Zarko Cosic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can we say of him, that he is, in a sense, your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: He lived near Draga, near the road down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You said today what he told your sister a couple of days prior to the events?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can we agree that what he said was that he would personally carry out the threat if anything happened to any of his family?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you recognised him as one of the persons who was in the village?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised him, because he was known by the nickname "Cigo" from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Today you mentioned the surname "Grubesic," but you used two first names. You mentioned "Nikica" and "Dusko." Do you have two different persons in mind?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Possibly Dusko Grubesic. I may have used the name "Nikica," but I meant "Dusko Grubesic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And who was Dusko Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: The commander of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You mean of the Busovaca Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. And who is Nikica, then, Nikica Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I may have been confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you made a mistake?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible that I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. If I understand you well, you are -- it is your conclusion that the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski in Busovaca Brigade gave the orders for the attack. That is your own conclusion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Nobody told you that explicitly, that he had given the order?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Surely, the soldiers wouldn't have themselves made this thing up if they hadn't been authorised to do what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you're telling us now that your conclusion is based on talks with various people following the event in April '93?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I was saying -- let me repeat my question. It is my mistake if you didn't understand me. It is your view and your conclusion that Dusko Grubesic issued that order on the basis of conversations you had subsequently with various people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, because when the shell fell close to Draga, when two persons were killed, Ivo Kristo said that the shell was coming from our side, that is, from above the Nuhagici village, and they started fleeing to Tisovac. But near the command at Tisovac, they were met and asked where they were going, and they said that there were shells coming from Ocehnici and Nuhagici, shells were coming aiming at Draga. Then Ivo Kristo said that they should go back, that there would be no more shells coming from Nuhagici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: How do you know these things, please?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I know because my brother was listening to a conversation when they turned them back from Busovaca. He told me that this was what Ivo Kristo had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And who told your brother?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: He heard it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You mean he was present?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were on the road, and his house was next to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when was this shelling of the Draga barracks? When did it take place; on what day?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: It was the same day, on the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, I understood what you had told us about that event, but I must tell you that when you made your statement to the Tribunal's investigators on the 10th of September, 1995, your first official statement to the investigators -- do you remember that first interview? I assume you do. You said, explicitly: "I read in a book that Dusko Grubesic was the commander of the Busovaca HVO and that he had ordered the attack on Ocehnici." You said this, that you had read it in a book, in your statement. I can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: That's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In view of these differences between what you said in your previous statement and what you said today, that in fact you don't know who had ordered the attack or, rather, you don't know where you got the information from?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question? If you didn't understand me, I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you allow for the possibility that you may have read that somewhere, can you agree with what I'm saying, that actually you don't know, with any precision, who had issued the order for the attack on your village, but you simply don't know who you heard it from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's consider whether that's going to help us very much. We've got the evidence that he said that on one occasion that he was told this, and he said that he read it, it's possible that he read it. Now, we've got the evidence, and it doesn't seem to me that any further cross-examination is going to take the case much further. If you would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I agree, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions about your stay in the village of Skradno. Mr. Nuhagic, you were in the village of Skradno from May until September of 1993; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: That's a mistake. Not from May but from the end of June or after the second half of June that we went to Skradno.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you said today "from August." Now you're saying "the second half of June." But I have to tell you that when you were interviewed or when you testified as a witness in the Blaskic case, on page 5237, lines 2 to 4, asked by the Prosecutor, you confirmed that you had been in Skradno roughly from May to September 1993. That is a quotation from your testimony in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I know that it was from the end of June. I didn't write those things, so that -- I didn't take note of those things so I could have the exact date. I never knew any of this would happen and I should keep a record. But the important thing is that I was there, and from Busovaca I was taken to Skradno.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you are allowing for the possibility that this may have been from May to September, as you said earlier on, testifying in Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I do not allow for that possibility, because I know I was sowing potatoes in Busovaca in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Then we can move on. You went to Zenica in September 1993 or, rather, you left Skradno in a so-called private exchange. That was an undercover exchange, as people used to call it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So this was your personal decision and the decision of your sons, who helped you in doing it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No, it was allowed. An illegal exchange was allowed. I think that that is what was said in Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If it was allowed, why would it be called illegal, then?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: The municipality, the police, nobody opposed the fighters of the HVO who were from the surroundings of Zenica, Travnik, or I don't know from where, for their families to be brought over and for us to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. I understand. Those were private arrangements?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, one could call them private.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Unofficial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: While you were in Busovaca, before going to Skradno, would you agree with me that there was a large influx of refugees, of Croats coming to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And those refugees exerted a great deal of pressure on the Muslims in particular but also on the Croats?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that the fighters, the soldiers, were those who were exerting the pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But, as you come from those parts, you know the locals. There were many soldiers who were driven out, not just their families?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Look here. Let me tell you. The people who put on a uniform, even the people I knew from a year before in Busovaca, once they put on a uniform, it is hard to -- we hardly knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were exposed to a certain amount of pressure in Busovaca, would you agree with me that in Skradno you were relatively better protected than in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No, it couldn't be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But nevertheless, we must agree, you were not exposed to so much pressure, not counting individual misdeeds, but generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I personally was not exposed to such pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when mention was made of Skradno, you said that people were taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you know, from what those people told you, where they went and what they did?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, because when a courier comes to pick them up, he says where they were going: to Kula, Bare, Strane.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you one thing about it. Those people who had this labour obligation, did they tell you that there were Croats working with them, and a few Serbs, those Croats who were unfit for military service?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. You repeated today, and I think you confirmed, that you rarely watch television, that you didn't have time for that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But nevertheless, you said that you remembered a few things. So you remember, I assume -- maybe that's a better way to put it. You testified about this in the Blaskic case, that is, about the people you saw on television, and you recounted things that you remembered from those programmes. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I don't remember very well; only the things I know about the president of the municipality and about Mr. Dario, the things I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but that's precisely where the difference is. In the Blaskic trial you remembered what Zoran Maric said, and what Anto Valenta said, on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you didn't remember any other event?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us comment briefly on what you said you heard Zoran Maric say on television. You said that this was when the swearing in of the HVO was taking place. Do you agree with me that that was in the second half of August 1992; it was in the summer?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly the months or the date, but I know very well when packets of cigarettes were being distributed to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Maric held a lengthy speech on that occasion. Do you remember that? It wasn't short.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Possibly, but I wasn't really interested. I wouldn't go into the house, unless one of the members of my household told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you didn't watch or listen to the whole speech delivered by Zoran Maric?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I have a few sentences from what he said. Perhaps that will refresh your memory. Let me read it out, briefly. Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Wait for me to read it out slowly, for the benefit of the interpreters. Do you remember Mr. Maric saying the following, and I quote: "We will fight for love, peace, and equality. That is precisely why we say it today, that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is not a community where other peoples will be second-rate citizens, but a community of love and equality." Do you remember these words?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on. Today you spoke about Mr. Dario Kordic, and you said that he was promoted gradually and he reached the rank of colonel. You don't know that from personal knowledge; you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So it was something that was being talked about in the village; you can't identify a specific person?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I didn't see his rank, but I heard tell that among the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If he moved up gradually to the rank of colonel, did you hear what rank he had before?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No. I just heard that he went up in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Mr. Nuhagic, that in fact you don't know explicitly which positions Mr. Kordic held from 1990 onwards?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: In 1990 he became an employee in the municipality. While he was in Vatrostalna, he was a reporter. He joined the Communist Party. And then he became an official in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And after he started working in the municipality, you don't really know what positions he held?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well, then. Then we won't go into that any further. As for Zoran Maric, we mentioned him a moment ago. You know that he was formally president of the municipality and the president of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I know he was president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you see on television, occasionally, reports from press conferences?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about these conferences, who spoke, and when, and so on?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Today, you said that you do remember seeing Mr. Kordic saying something about potatoes on television?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Where were you when you were watching this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: In Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: What kind of a programme was that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: They had a meeting without TV cameras. When they finished the meeting, then Miro Dzakula would go to the municipality, and I remember this was stated publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, who was Miro Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: He was some sort of a donator. He would treat them, when they had meetings, with refreshments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: What kind of meetings? At the municipality? At what level?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: In the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And this feature that you watched, what was it about, on television?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I couldn't tell you. I don't know what the topic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In view of the fact that Mr. Kordic personally had nothing to do with humanitarian aid, I have to tell you that Mr. Kordic never spoke about any such things. So my question is: Are you quite sure that he said that, rather than somebody else that you saw on television?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: And this was at the end of the meeting, when he was interviewed by television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. My question was a bit different. Are you sure that it was Mr. Kordic who spoke about humanitarian aid, and not someone else? For instance, do you know who headed the Red Cross in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I do not know, but I know that the potato came through humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. There were two questions there. One at a time, so the witness can deal with them. It's now eleven. Have you got many more questions for this witness, Mr. Naumovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think in some 15 or 20 minutes I could finish, maybe earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour explain the position to the witness about contact, because there is no interpreter available for me to explain that to him, and it -- and maybe he hasn't been told beforehand of what the regime is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't usually mention it in this adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, may we resume? Let us just round off the topic that we were talking about before. While in Busovaca, did you know one Stipo Santic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now, as I have said, you did not answer the question that I asked you before the break, so I have to repeat it. So are you quite sure that it was not somebody else who spoke on the subject of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I don't really know why you are so interested in those potatoes and humanitarian aid. Municipal authorities know all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the point. I think you've dealt pretty thoroughly with that, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now, let us move on, since we've touched upon Mr. Kordic. Mr. Nuhagic, tell me, please, did you ever meet and come to know Mr. Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, when I was with Hasija Beslic, when she was telling him about those documents that he was issuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Would you tell us, please, who is Hasija Beslic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Hasija Beslic? Well, she's just a woman who used to work at the Vatrostalna in Busovaca with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Where did she live; in the town?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: In the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Until when was she in Busovaca? Is she still there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No. She left in the month of September, as everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And where was it that you met Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Opposite the so-called hardware store or the department store. There's a church there and just a small square, a small triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And what were you doing in the town on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I was walking with that Hasija, whom I knew from before, because a neighbour from the village that I knew was staying in the neighbouring house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And did you see the kind of permit or certificate that she had and who signed it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Sir, I had such a certificate, and all the people of Muslim ethnicity. Let's not talk too much about that certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not saying you did not have a certificate. I'm just saying the Court saw different signatories on such certificates. Some were signed by Mr. Maric, some by Dusko Grubesic. And my question was what kind of a certificate this lady had and whose name was signed there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. She said the types of certificates were issued so as not to be disturbed by Croat troops, because they are worthless.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But that conversation that you are talking about, it involved Hasija Beslic, and you were only present there; is that so?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: She complained that she was being harassed, disturbed by troops, and you say that she said Mr. Kordic said that it would not happen again?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And after that conversation, do you know what happened then to Hasija Beslic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, we parted our ways, because she went home and I also went to the place where I was staying in Busovaca on a different street.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No. What I wanted to ask you was: Do you know if soldiers came again to her place?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Does that mean that you saw her on different occasions?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I mean, today you mentioned only one conversation with her. That is why I'm asking you that. When you were present at that conversation, could you tell us, was there somebody else present? Was Mr. Kordic alone?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Completely alone, all by himself?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. You don't know where he was coming from, where he was headed; you don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And I agree with you. I believe I understood you well. You did not mention your case, where you lived, what you were, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you say that after that conversation, soldiers came again to the place where you were and said or, rather, showed that they did not like your having a complaint to Kordic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, and Hasija did the same thing. I didn't show the certificate, but she was safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nuhagic, let us try to be quite precise. Today, when asked by the Prosecution, you answered that soldiers came to your house and said that you complained to Kordic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, to my place, and Hasija's, and everybody else. "You complained to Kordic about those certificates that you have, but they are worth nothing. He knows about all this, that you are being disturbed, and about everything else."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I get your point. But will you try to distinguish between when you talked with Hasija later on and what you personally know? So will you tell us, when the troops came to your house, what did they exactly tell you, you personally?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Me, personally, and to one of my relatives, a second, third relative of mine, when we would show the documents, they say, "They are worthless. You went to complain to Kordic, Hasija Beslic, and everybody else, but whoever does that, we don't."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I must ask you this once again. You said explicitly today that those troops said to you that you went to complain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That has been said several times. Now, we've got the point.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask to go back not to some questions, because there are various paragraphs and items here. Let us follow those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us decide how the questioning is done here, but we'll make sure that you aren't harassed by going back over old matter. Yes. Have you got very much more, Mr. Naumovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, will you agree with me on one point: You gave two statements to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you also gave a statement to the Zenica police in 1994?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So it means three. And you also testified on two occasions: in the Blaskic case and in the Aleksovski case. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So it was five times that you gave the statements?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So will you agree with me that on no one occasion in any of those statements, or in your testimony before the Court, did you mention the conversation with Hasija Beslic and the humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, that was in '94, or '95, when I made that statement. Perhaps it simply -- I simply didn't remember that, because what I told you -- I mean, the record would not show everything that one says, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No. But, very briefly, can we agree that you never mentioned that before, that this is the first time that you mentioned it, in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nuhagic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My name is Goran Mikulicic, and with my learned friend, Mr. Kovacic, I represent the second accused, Mario Cerkez. Now, first I should like to express my sincere sympathies, condolences to you, for all the losses that you suffered during the events in Busovaca. Now, Mr. Nuhagic, let us go back to 1992 for a while, when the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was attacked. At that time, sometime in mid-1992, Busovaca was attacked too, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, but with that Mario Cerkez, I heard about him now here, at the hearing that he was part. And as when I was preparing, I was told that, but as I said, I had nothing to do with him, because he did not come from my municipality, that Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nuhagic, we understand that, because you are from the municipality of Busovaca, and all that you said refers to that municipality, does it not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But I shall be very brief, so will you please try to answer it. Is it true that sometime in mid-1992, Busovaca was shelled by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And as a village inhabitant, like your neighbours, did you think that you might be attacked by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was shelled. Even Draga, which was quite near me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Nuhagic, did you undertake any measures to protect yourselves in the village?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Only a shelter. When the alert would go on, then we would go downstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But apart from that, did the villagers organise themselves; that is, did you go on guard to take -- to be on the alert, to see that the attack --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Not in 1992, when the shelling happened, because there was no need for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And later on, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Oh, well, in '92, but it was very late in '92 we had some guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you had your village guards, which you organised yourselves, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Nuhagic, and those village guards, were they armed with anything?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, a hunting rifle, a carbine and something -- something automatic, those drum rifles or Kalasnikovs. I don't know what they are called, but they came from the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But could you remember, because it was a long time ago, how many pieces of weapons did the village guards in the village have?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Five pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And those village guards, Mr. Nuhagic, did they receive orders from somebody?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it was organised in the village, and they -- there were neighbours, Croats, so we had contact with them in '92, in late '92, and in the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But did those village guards have a commander?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, no. Only we who were in that village. I don't know about others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were you also one of the village guards, Mr. Nuhagic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Nuhagic, I have no further questions. Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, you've been asked about saying in your -- one of your statements to the Tribunal investigators that you read in a book about Grubesic, Dusko, being the commander of the Busovaca HVO, and ordering Ljubicic, Pasko, to attack the village. You've also given us an account of how you learnt of that from your brother. When, after the attack, did you first meet your brother? How many hours or days later was it that you met him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it was two or three later, that we were in Busovaca, and he was there too, and that is when he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, we've taken the awful experiences you suffered very shortly, in the interest of saving time, and partly in the interests of saving your feelings. But you met your brother two or three hours or two or three days later?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: The next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next day. And he then told you what you've told us today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And is it right that before you made the statement to the Office of the Prosecutor investigators, you had made a statement to the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM NUHAGIC
utterances.text: I did give some statements, but that was a long time ago, and I cannot really remember it all. And besides, we were still afraid of the war and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I, rather than go through the exercise of putting a document before the witness, read to the Court, and my friends have got it to follow, that in that statement he sets out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you identify the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's an official record written on the 26th of March of 1994, according to the record itself, based on an interview conducted with this witness. And it's at the second page in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what the witness told the investigators was that: "The Croat population from the area..."
